reviewerOrPass: Worker A, same AI, separate source-first pass
method: Same AI, separate source-first pass after freezing. Started with the cohort-specific OER tables and thesis and atelier requirements, then independently checked the workbook for Frisian coverage and reconsidered the actual contributions in language acquisition, literature, heritage and policy. Rechecked the three schedules and all positive and blank alignments against the frozen record.
findings: The 2026–2027 OER for Nederlandse Talen en Culturen identifies Frisian Language and Culture as the separate, target-named FTC track. Articles 4.1.1b and 5.1.1c close at 60 EC per year. The first year combines the shared literature and linguistics units with Frisian Studies, standard language and use, and a faculty choice. Year 2 combines Frisian and shared study. The autumn Year 3 minor is followed by a faculty choice, the thesis and an internship, worth 10 EC each. Do not stack predecessor cohorts, the Dutch track or the separate Frisian minor. The OER explicitly defers the new cohort’s Year 2 and Year 3 listings to their later catalogue years. Dutch or Frisian are the track languages, with English permissible for some courses.

The first year combines foundations in sound systems, syntax, semantics, cognition and interpretation with entry into Frisian studies. Year 2 deepens language use, literature, regional study, language acquisition and research. The OER requires ateliers in both literature and linguistics. Article 7.1 requires at least 50 EC from year one, 100 EC in the BA and completion of Research Approaches before the thesis for this cohort. The full first two years and Research Approaches meet the requirement before the spring thesis. Article 3.2 calls for the language of the track for the thesis and permits a different language outside Dutch or Frisian only with board permission. The internship is a separate 10 EC component.

The closest option directly responds to language study through introductory Dutch, stylistics and cognitive poetics, and psycholinguistics with bilingualism, language acquisition and speech. Rhetoric and applied communication support the public use of language. Sociology and qualitative methods provide genuine contexts and methods for investigating language in society. The literature and media option has its own progression in interpretation, literary genres, memoir, adaptation and documentary. Description-only Renaissance Italy and Writing Art’s Histories add comparative visual culture and methods of interpretation. The third option responds to public culture and regional institutions through museum practice, collections and restitution, cultural heritage, comparative politics, policy analysis and social theory. Public Policy Analysis provides a real description-supported contribution in comparative policy processes and policy writing. It does not teach Frisian language policy. American media and history courses supply contextual methods, not regional Frisian evidence. These three substantive strands differ in central questions, core selections and methods. The workbook has no Frisian instruction or sustained Frisian studies, and beginner Dutch, bilingualism and literary work cannot implement the separate Frisian-specific direction. Rescheduling Psycholinguistics after Brain and Behavior and moving Rhetoric in Action to an offered term repair the closest option. The two more specific options retain literary or public-institution focus through academically stronger substitutions. Kept only three supported partial alignments, with the local thesis, internship and language specialism displayed separately.
